references.text: God announces that He will wipe out humans, animals, creeping things, and birds from the face of the earth—a direct prophetic prediction fulfilled in Gen 7:21.
God warns that He will bring a flood upon the earth to destroy all flesh that has the breath of life under heaven—fulfilled in Gen 7:21.
The continuation of the description of destruction: everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died, and God wiped out everything that was on the earth.
Describes how creatures die when God takes back their spirit, a thematic parallel to the universal death in the flood.
The world at that time was destroyed by water—a direct New Testament reference to the flood's destruction of all life.
By faith Noah built an ark for the salvation of his household, and through this he condemned the world—an indirect reference to the destruction that struck all flesh.
Jesus refers to the days of Noah: they ate and drank until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
This reference highlights the theological symmetry between judgment and restoration in the flood narrative.
The reference illuminates the contrast between those saved into the ark and those wiped out outside it, using an identical list of creatures.
This connection shows the transition from judgment to God's new covenant with the same creatures that survived.
The reference highlights the direct narrative opposition between destruction in Gen 7:21 and the command for restoration in Gen 8:17.
Job 34:15 illuminates the theological reason for the destruction in Gen 7:21: that God's spirit is withdrawn from all flesh.
The reference shows the dramatic contrast between the creation of these animals in Gen 1:24 and their total destruction in Gen 7:21.
This reference highlights the contrast between God's gift of life and food in Gen 1:30 and the judgment upon all life in Gen 7:21.
Romans 5:12 provides the theological explanation for the historical destruction in Gen 7:21: death as a consequence of sin affects everyone.
7:21 is a historical example of the principle in Romans 2:12: that all who have sinned must die.
